intro.headline: India in 1900
intro.summary: Highlights of this year's checked items: The famine of 1899-1900; 200 metres silver, Paris; Bose's millimetre radio waves; Rabindranath Tagore; Viceroy: Lord Curzon; Haffkine's plague vaccine.

technology-science.title: Technology & science
technology-science.standfirst: In this section: Railways: about 25,400 miles open; Haffkine's plague vaccine; Bose's millimetre radio waves; Inland money orders.

items.title: Railways: about 25,400 miles open
items.summary: The Gazetteer's table of railway mileage open for traffic gives a total of about 25,400 miles for 1901, mostly on the broad (5 ft 6 in) and metre gauges.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. III: Economic (1907), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

items.title: Haffkine's plague vaccine
items.summary: Waldemar Haffkine tested his plague vaccine on himself in Bombay in January 1897. By the turn of the century about four million people in India had received it.

items.title: Bose's millimetre radio waves
items.summary: In Calcutta in 1895 Jagadish Chandra Bose rang a bell and fired gunpowder from across a room with millimetre-wavelength waves. In 1900 he presented his research at the International Congress of Physics in Paris.

items.title: Inland money orders
items.summary: The post office issued 12,922,465 inland money orders in 1900-01, worth about Rs 26 crore, up from 7.3 million orders ten years earlier.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. III: Economic (1907), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

government-politics.title: Government & politics
government-politics.standfirst: In this section: Viceroy: Lord Curzon; Secretary of State for India; Legislative councils after 1892; Punjab Alienation of Land Act; Princely states.

items.title: Viceroy: Lord Curzon
items.summary: George Nathaniel Curzon took office as Viceroy and Governor-General in January 1899 and headed the Government of India through 1900.

sources.label: Wikipedia: George Curzon, 1st Marquess Curzon of Kedleston

items.title: Secretary of State for India
items.summary: Under the Act of 1858 the Secretary of State was the Crown's constitutional adviser on India, helped by a Council that he was not usually bound to follow. Lord George Hamilton held the post from July 1895.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. IV: Administrative (1909), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive
Wikipedia: Secretary of State for India

items.title: Legislative councils after 1892
items.summary: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 enlarged the supreme and provincial legislative councils, introduced the elective element tentatively and allowed members to question the government and discuss the budget.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. IV: Administrative (1909), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

items.title: Punjab Alienation of Land Act
items.summary: The 1900 Act limited the sale of farmland in Punjab to members of notified 'agricultural tribes'. It was meant to stop land passing from peasants to moneylenders and was resented by many educated Hindus.

items.title: Princely states
items.summary: A large part of India was ruled by hereditary chiefs in 'native states' under British paramountcy. The Government of India's policy was generally not to interfere in their internal affairs.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. IV: Administrative (1909), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

law.title: A law in 1900: the Punjab Alienation of Land Bill

steps.label: Introduced
steps.detail: On 27 September 1899 Charles Rivaz presented a proposal titled the Punjab Alienation of Land Bill to the Imperial Legislative Council.

steps.label: Debated
steps.detail: Educated Hindus in the province saw it as discrimination; Congress delegates at Lucknow in 1899 supported opposition to it.

steps.label: Enacted
steps.detail: It became the Punjab Alienation of Land Act, 1900.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Secretary of State for India
Wikipedia: George Curzon, 1st Marquess Curzon of Kedleston

freedom-history.title: Independence & history
freedom-history.standfirst: In this section: The famine of 1899-1900; Birsa Munda and the Ulgulan; Congress meets at Lahore; Indian stretcher-bearers in the Boer War.

items.title: The famine of 1899-1900
items.summary: The 1899 monsoon failed over the west and centre of India. At the end of July 1900 no fewer than 6,500,000 people were on daily relief, and the Famine Commission of 1901 thought about a million deaths in British districts could be attributed to it.

sensitivity.note: Describes mass death by famine and disease.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. III: Economic (1907), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

items.title: Birsa Munda and the Ulgulan
items.summary: Birsa Munda led a millenarian movement among the Munda people of the Bengal Presidency (now Jharkhand). He was arrested in February 1900 and died in jail in June 1900, after which the movement faded.

sensitivity.note: Armed conflict, police firing and death in custody.

items.title: Congress meets at Lahore
items.summary: The sixteenth annual session of the Indian National Congress met at Lahore in December 1900 with N. G. Chandavarkar as president.

sources.label: Wikipedia: List of presidents of the Indian National Congress

items.title: Indian stretcher-bearers in the Boer War
items.summary: In Natal, Mohandas Gandhi helped raise an ambulance corps of about 1,100 Indian volunteers for the British side in the Boer War. It was disbanded after Ladysmith was relieved at the end of February 1900.

sensitivity.note: A war, with casualties on all sides.

personalities.title: Famous personalities
personalities.standfirst: In this section: Jagadish Chandra Bose; Swami Vivekananda; Rabindranath Tagore; Birsa Munda; Norman Pritchard.

items.title: Jagadish Chandra Bose
items.summary: Physicist and plant scientist, born at Mymensingh in 1858.
items.whyThisYear: He presented his radio-wave research at the International Congress of Physics in Paris and was turning to plant physiology.

items.title: Swami Vivekananda
items.summary: Monk and teacher, born in Calcutta in 1863.
items.whyThisYear: He travelled to Paris for the Congress of Religions in 1900 during his second visit to the West.

items.title: Rabindranath Tagore
items.summary: Bengali poet, born in Calcutta in 1861.
items.whyThisYear: 1900 is the publication year of four of his books: Katha, Kahini, Kalpana and Kshanika.

sources.label: Wikipedia: List of works by Rabindranath Tagore

items.title: Birsa Munda
items.summary: Tribal leader, born in 1875 near Ranchi.
items.whyThisYear: He was arrested in February and died in jail in June 1900.

items.title: Norman Pritchard
items.summary: Calcutta-born sprinter and hurdler (1875 to 1929).
items.whyThisYear: He won silver in the 200 m and the 200 m hurdles at the Paris Olympics; the IOC credits the medals to India.

items.title: Waldemar Haffkine
items.summary: Odessa-born bacteriologist who worked in Bombay (1860 to 1930).
items.whyThisYear: He received the Cameron Prize of the University of Edinburgh and became a British subject in 1900.

items.title: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
items.summary: Lawyer from Porbandar, born in 1869, living in South Africa.
items.whyThisYear: His stretcher-bearer corps served in Natal in the Boer War until Ladysmith was relieved.

items.title: Ranjitsinhji
items.summary: Cricketer born in Kathiawar in 1872, later Jam Sahib of Nawanagar.
items.whyThisYear: He scored 3,065 runs for Sussex in the 1900 English season.

achievements.title: Achievements
achievements.standfirst: In this section: First Olympic medals credited to India; Four million plague vaccinations; Radio-wave research shown in Paris; Saraswati, a Hindi monthly.

items.title: First Olympic medals credited to India
items.summary: Norman Pritchard's two silver medals in Paris in 1900 are the first Olympic medals credited to India by the IOC.

items.title: Four million plague vaccinations
items.summary: By the turn of the century about four million people in India had received Haffkine's plague vaccine.

items.title: Radio-wave research shown in Paris
items.summary: Bose took his Calcutta radio-wave experiments to the first International Congress of Physics in Paris in 1900.

items.title: Saraswati, a Hindi monthly
items.summary: Saraswati, founded in 1900 by Chintamani Ghosh at the Indian Press in Allahabad, is described as the first Hindi monthly magazine of India.

sports.title: Sports
sports.standfirst: In this section: 200 metres silver, Paris; 200 metres hurdles silver, Paris; Ranjitsinhji's 3,065 runs; Bengal's 100 yards champion.

items.title: 200 metres silver, Paris
items.summary: Norman Pritchard finished second in the first Olympic 200 m, in 22.8 seconds behind Walter Tewksbury's 22.2.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Athletics at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Men's 200 metres

items.title: 200 metres hurdles silver, Paris
items.summary: Pritchard won his heat in 26.8 and took silver in the final behind Al Kraenzlein, who won in 25.4.
items.scoreline: Winner 25.4 s; Pritchard about five yards behind

items.title: Ranjitsinhji's 3,065 runs
items.summary: Ranjitsinhji scored 3,065 runs at 87.57 for Sussex in the 1900 English county season, the second highest aggregate to that point and top of the national averages.

items.title: Bengal's 100 yards champion
items.summary: Pritchard won the Bengal 100 yards title seven years running, 1894 to 1900, and was also provincial champion at 440 yards and 120 yards hurdles.

steps.label: Heat 2
steps.text: Pritchard wins in 26.8, an Olympic record, with Walter Tewksbury two yards behind; both advance.

steps.label: Final
steps.text: Al Kraenzlein wins in 25.4 by about five yards despite a false-start penalty.

steps.label: Medals
steps.text: Pritchard takes silver; Tewksbury is third, about a yard further back.

books-reading.title: Books & reading
books-reading.standfirst: In this section: Saraswati; Open Letters to Lord Curzon on Famines and Land Assessments in India; The Civilization of India; Kim, in serial.

items.title: Saraswati
items.summary: A Hindi monthly founded in 1900 at the Indian Press, Allahabad. Under Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi (editor 1903 to 1920) it shaped modern Hindi prose and poetry.
items.creator: Chintamani Ghosh (proprietor)

items.title: Open Letters to Lord Curzon on Famines and Land Assessments in India
items.summary: R. C. Dutt, a retired civil servant, addressed open letters to the Viceroy arguing that land-revenue demands deepened famines. The book was published in London in 1900.
items.creator: Romesh Chunder Dutt

items.title: The Civilization of India
items.summary: R. C. Dutt's survey of India's civilisation was published in 1900.
items.creator: Romesh Chunder Dutt

items.title: Kim, in serial
items.summary: Rudyard Kipling's Kim began its serial run in McClure's Magazine in December 1900, a portrait of India by a British author.
items.creator: Rudyard Kipling

cinema.title: Cinema
cinema.standfirst: In this section: Moving pictures reach Bombay; The Wrestlers (1899); A Man and His Monkeys (1899); Hiralal Sen films The Flower of Persia (1898).

items.title: Moving pictures reach Bombay
items.summary: The Lumière brothers' films were shown in Bombay in 1896, the same year they travelled the world.

items.title: The Wrestlers (1899)
items.summary: Harishchandra Sakharam Bhatavdekar filmed a wrestling match in Bombay in 1899, described as the first film shot by an Indian.
items.notable: Among the first films shot by an Indian

items.title: A Man and His Monkeys (1899)
items.summary: Bhatavdekar's second 1899 film recorded a man with his trained monkeys.

items.title: Hiralal Sen films The Flower of Persia (1898)
items.summary: In 1898 Hiralal Sen filmed scenes of the stage show The Flower of Persia at a Calcutta theatre and founded the Royal Bioscope company.

cinema.scarcityNote: No Indian film dated to 1900 itself was found in the sources opened; the items below are the earliest Indian film activity those sources describe.

music-arts.title: Music & arts
music-arts.standfirst: In this section: Raja Deen Dayal, photographer; Raja Ravi Varma Press; Parsi theatre; Mysore Palace under construction.

items.title: Raja Deen Dayal, photographer
items.summary: Lala Deen Dayal, court photographer to the Nizam of Hyderabad since 1885 and holder of a Royal Warrant from Queen Victoria since 1897, was at work from studios in Hyderabad and Bombay.
items.creator: Lala Deen Dayal

items.title: Raja Ravi Varma Press
items.summary: Raja Ravi Varma's lithographic press, started in Bombay in 1894, moved to Malavli near Lonavala in 1899 and made oleograph prints of Hindu gods and epic scenes.
items.creator: Raja Ravi Varma

items.title: Parsi theatre
items.summary: Parsi theatre companies, mostly performing in Urdu and Gujarati, toured western and northern India; some producers turned to bioscope in the early 1900s.

items.title: Mysore Palace under construction
items.summary: After the old palace burned down, Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV commissioned a new palace in August 1897 from the architect Henry Irwin; it was completed in 1912.
items.creator: Henry Irwin

economy-business.title: Economy & business
economy-business.standfirst: In this section: Population; Rupee exchange rate.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The 1901 Census counted 294 million people in India.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. IV: Administrative (1909), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive

items.title: Rupee exchange rate
items.summary: By 1899-1900 the rupee had reached the rate of 1s 4d, the goal of government policy; 15 rupees equalled one pound.

sources.label: The Imperial Gazetteer of India, The Indian Empire, vol. IV: Administrative (1909), Oxford, Clarendon Press, via the Internet Archive
